title: Corpse or creature
proposal: The 'body' could be a corpse, boss or creature. 'What remains' would be physical remains, loot or fragments after its death. Assembly would use a named surviving drop or set.
support: The hunt starts with Frozen Corpse loot, and many creatures leave recoverable drops. This is the literal reading of body/remains.
weakness: Almost every mob fits. No named creature or recipe is identified.
test_coverage: R011: Not tested | R014: Partially tested | R021: Tested negative under specified conditions | R040: Tested negative under specified conditions
verify_next: Find a clue selecting one entity and a distinct remaining drop.
assessment: I think it's a sensible literal reading, but too broad for another random drop test.

title: Soul, ghost or surviving effect
proposal: The physical creature disappears, but a soul, spirit, buff or temporary effect remains.
support: 'Body is not enough' contrasts physical and intangible survival.
weakness: Most soul-related items have broad negative tests; no assembly target.
test_coverage: R037: Partially tested | R062: Partially tested | R072: Tested negative under specified conditions | R075: Tested negative under specified conditions

assessment: I would reopen this only if we find an actual survivor and how to combine it.

proposal: Two related but different hypotheses: a reported large shadow over Great Glacite Lake is a clue to a 'body', or actual local light level / light-state transition is a hidden R6 condition. Shadow appearance and numeric light level must not be treated as equivalent.

weakness: No original image is linked here or reproduced under controlled conditions. Night Vision affects rendering rather than actual light level, and no R6 response to light was reported.
test_coverage: N012: Partially tested | R024: Partially tested | R041: Partially tested | R009: Partially tested
verify_next: Recover the original screenshot; repeat from a fixed camera position with and without Night Vision. Independently measure actual block light at chosen locations and compare Journal status; don't spend items without a selected second action.
assessment: I want to distinguish a graphic effect from a reproducible light-level state before requesting another item test.

title: R1: Chestplate reveals the Journal
proposal: The first Hunt step consumes the Dead Man's Chestplate in Great Glacite Lake and exposes the hidden Journal. R6 might echo this container-and-survivor relationship: when one 'body' vanishes, another object is revealed.
support: R1 establishes an actual Hunt interaction in which an outer item disappears and a concealed item survives. This is directly relevant to interpreting 'body' and 'remains', unlike a loose item-name match.
weakness: The Journal emerges already complete, not assembled from parts. R1's positive result does not prove another R6 container, crafting requirement, or hidden object exists.
test_coverage: The R1 sequence was recorded succeeding; later Chestplate/Journal offerings were reported without a new advancement. Those later offerings are narrower than any newly identified R6 container hypothesis.
verify_next: Identify a second explicitly concealed or composite object in current lore before suggesting a new offering; treat the earlier R1 demonstration as precedent rather than solution evidence.
assessment: Confirmed R1; R6 continuation unverified

proposal: The solved item initials read D E F A G. Removing F and rearranging the rest gives AGED, but both choices need justification. DEFAG playback was reported on October 11.

test_coverage: October 11 musical playback is reported; later November 13 mixed music/event trials are separate. Removing F and making AGED is an unmotivated extra step.

title: R4 arrivals, R5 presence and proposed R6 absence
proposal: R4 checks three separate arrivals within roughly ten seconds. R5 succeeds with three Calling units already present, then a Griffin Feather. Their recordings are separate. An R6 absence stage is a further hypothesis.
support: R4 and R5 demonstrably check different aspects of offerings: repeated arrivals versus pre-existing units plus a later arrival.
weakness: R5 also contains an arrival, and R1 already contains disappearance. No progression rule into R6 is proven.
test_coverage: Alpha R4 used two normal Callings and a recombobulated third; only the triggering one vanished. Alpha R5 used a fresh stack of three, then a Feather; the completed Journal is visible at 5.9s. No separate R5 reward is identified.
verify_next: Require a selected remnant and assembly before extrapolating to absence. R5 also has an arrival, while R1 already has disappearance; this is not a proven three-stage law.
assessment: I accept the R4/R5 distinction and keep the proposed R6 absence step speculative.

title: Replaying the R1–R5 procedures
proposal: Replay R1–R5 with their original conditions. October 7 combination proposals predate the public R6 clue; later mixed repeat tests are not a documented complete reenactment.
support: The Journal preserves earlier successful procedures, including position, distance, repeated arrivals and prior item presence.
weakness: No clue asks for a restart. A stage-perfect replay and its Journal result were not established.
test_coverage: October 7 proposals can predate R6. Later mixed offerings do not document a stage-perfect replay with all checkpoints.
verify_next: Find an instruction selecting which old actions to repeat. A complete reenactment would need exact order and Journal before/after, not a bag of old items.
assessment: I see no instruction to restart the chain, so I would not repeat all five steps blindly.

title: ARK-style taming and an unseen lake creature
proposal: Read the earlier offerings as gaining an unseen lake creature's trust, sometimes compared with ARK taming. Feeding, distance and repeated calling give it a coherent story.
support: Feeding, distance and repeated calls can be read as interacting with an unseen creature rather than decoding independent items.
weakness: No creature, trust counter or distinct R6 prediction has been observed. Discussion alone was not a gameplay test.
test_coverage: The source record contains an ARK analogy and feeding interpretations, not an observed creature, trust meter or controlled taming result.
verify_next: Look for an independent NPC, entity response or changed interaction that predicts the next action before naming a food.
assessment: I like the coherent story, but an analogy without a detectable creature is not a testable solution.

title: Repeated Calling cycles
proposal: Treat the individual Callings as part of larger narrative call cycles, then look for a third cycle. Calling/Crystal repetitions were reported, with uneven outcome records.
support: Repetition is genuinely part of R4, so a larger sequence of calls is mechanically conceivable.
weakness: R4 already triggers on the third arrival. No separate cycle counter or chosen next action.
test_coverage: Calling/Crystal repetition reports vary in quantities and outcomes. They do not establish a separate three-cycle counter.
verify_next: Recover the exact reported cycle and its outcome; identify what makes a full cycle distinct from one accepted arrival.
assessment: I would reopen this only if a source defines the larger cycle.

title: Earlier offerings surviving and despawning
proposal: October 8 reports include letting three Callings despawn while a Feather remains, then offering Stick and Ancient Claw. Other procedures waited for all four offerings to disappear.
support: R5 explicitly selects pre-existing offerings. Later disappearance could therefore be a meaningful variable to isolate.
weakness: These are performed-procedure reports, not complete Journal negatives. Despawn, pickup and quest consumption differ.
test_coverage: messup: Oct 8 03:34, all four despawn then three Iron Ingots + Enchanted Ice; 23:12, all despawn then Stick/Feather or Stick/Flint; 23:16, Callings gone but Feather present then Stick + Ancient Claw. Outcomes and stage captures are unspecified.
verify_next: Distinguish natural despawn, pickup and quest consumption. The old waits were performed; a missing outcome is not a negative or an untouched opportunity.
assessment: I retain these as real procedure reports, but they select no surviving component or assembly.

title: Correct item with a missing condition
proposal: The correct item might need an extra location, timing, equipment or player state. Earlier steps demonstrate mixed requirements, and many conditional throws have already been reported.
support: R2–R5 show that a correct item can need another location, distance, timing, count or presence condition.
weakness: This is a testing framework. It identifies neither the object nor the extra condition.
test_coverage: Many multi-condition offerings exist. Their different loadouts and incomplete stage checks cannot be merged into one universal negative.
verify_next: Choose a condition from a specific source first, then compare the exact prior procedure. Incomplete coverage alone does not justify a new test.
assessment: I use this as a test-design framework, not as evidence that a particular failed item is secretly correct.

title: Journal possession, replacement and unlocked progress
proposal: Separate the physical Journal from unlocked progress. On November 13 JJSR reported buying a second Journal from Rusty: different UUID, same solved riddles. This is a firsthand report, not footage of losing and replacing the original.
support: R1 leaves an intact readable Journal; JJSR's November 13 second-copy report supports solved information surviving a change of item UUID.
weakness: The report supports progress surviving a Journal UUID change. It does not establish private server implementation, full loss/recovery, an extraction rule or any R6 trigger.
test_coverage: Oct 7 storage/progression reports and Oct 13 disposal/repurchase reports are separate. JJSR, Nov 13 03:54: second Rusty Journal had a different UUID but the same solved riddles. No attached before/after recording was found in the inspected 03:51–03:59 discussion.
verify_next: Check an existing paired-item/Journal-menu capture if one becomes available. Do not destroy the original or infer server architecture from the UUID report.
assessment: I give the second-copy observation more weight than the older no-outcome purchase report; I still have no selected R6 assembly action.

title: The Dead Man's unidentified origin
proposal: The Chestplate owner, looted corpse, Journal writer and person described by the riddles might be different people. R1 confirms the hidden Journal, not a named identity.
support: The Chestplate, a Frozen Corpse and an anonymous Journal are concrete Hunt objects whose ownership could supply a selector.
weakness: No inscription or dialogue identifies the Dead Man. Lore discussion alone cannot test the identity.
test_coverage: Identity discussions and look-alike corpse theories are not experiments establishing who wrote the Journal.
verify_next: Seek a named inscription, dialogue or authenticated item history linking writer, armor owner and corpse; preserve the possibility that they differ.
assessment: I would prioritize a direct identity source over another object merely associated with death.

title: Divan's identity and lost kingdom
proposal: Dulin calls himself a descendant of Divan and the rightful king; this supplies a real historical/lore connection to the Glacite region, not an identification of the Dead Man. A Divan expedition member or associated dwarf remains a possible Journal owner. Divan-gear and corpse-perk procedures have been reported, but none identifies the writer.
support: Dulin's claim of descent and kingship provides actual regional lore rather than a similarity of item names.
weakness: A player dying with corpse perks is not a Frozen Corpse loot event. No source names Divan as the Journal's owner.
test_coverage: Divan gear, corpse-perk and related offerings were reported. They do not identify the Journal writer or reproduce looting a Frozen Corpse.
verify_next: Find a line explicitly linking Divan or an expedition member to the Chestplate/Journal; distinguish wearer death from corpse loot generation.
assessment: I keep the lore connection, but I do not call Divan the Dead Man.

title: Dulin, Sor'Hen and succession
proposal: Dulin and Sor'Hen connect the missing king with surviving artifacts. Dulin's remains/assembly wording belongs to Railroad Pass progression. Four-player Dulin/Grandpa dialogue procedures were reported October 31.
support: Dulin's progression involves surviving materials; Sor'Hen explicitly seeks artifacts and knowledge about the lost king.
weakness: Ordinary quest wording and a group conversation do not establish a Hunt trigger or an event-ending test.
test_coverage: The prior record reports four-player Dulin/Grandpa dialogue procedures on October 31. That is group interaction coverage, not an event-ending trial.
verify_next: Quote the exact quest condition and ordinary exchange before claiming its wording is a Hunt hint.
assessment: I treat the real dialogue as background until it selects a distinct R6 operation.

title: Reconstruction from Frozen Corpse loot
proposal: Assemble something from Frozen Corpse loot after the body is retrieved. Reports include Tungsten and Lapis conversion chains. Caged Wisp to Will-o-wisp is a real Forge route; direct Chestplate salvage was refused.
support: The Hunt begins in Frozen Corpse loot, and that loot can feed actual Forge and material-conversion recipes.
weakness: No loot type or recipe is selected. A complete R6-active Wisp chain is not established by generic Forge claims.
